why: A chain is an increasing sequence by word length in which each word is the previous one with one letter deleted: LIS where 'can follow' means 'is a one-deletion predecessor'. Sort by length and let best[w] = 1 + max best[w with one letter removed].
hints: Each step removes exactly one letter, so word lengths in a chain go down by exactly 1. Process short words first.
best[w] = length of the longest chain ending at w (read from short to long). For each w, try deleting each of its letters; if that shorter word is in the dictionary, best[w] can be best[shorter] + 1.
Sort the words by length, store best in a hash map, and try all len(w) deletions per word. O(N * L^2) time for N words of length up to L; the answer is the largest best value.
pitfalls: A single word with no valid predecessor still forms a chain of length 1.
Deleting different letters can give the same word (e.g. 'aab'); that is fine, just take the max.
Duplicate words in the input should not lengthen a chain.
Only words in the dictionary count; 'bads' -> 'bad' fails because 'bad' is not in the list.
statement:
You are given a dictionary words. Starting from any word, you may repeatedly delete exactly one letter, but every word you produce must also be in the dictionary. The words visited form a chain.

Return the length (number of words) of the longest chain that can be formed.

Example: words = ["bac", "ac", "a", "c", "bads"].

  1. Start from "bac" and delete b: "ac" is in the dictionary.
  2. Delete c from "ac": "a" is in the dictionary.
  3. "a" cannot shrink further, so the chain bac -> ac -> a has 3 words.
  4. "bads" cannot start a chain longer than 1: none of ads, bds, bas, bad is in the dictionary.

The answer is 3.
constraints:
• 1 <= words.length <= 10^4
  • 1 <= words[i].length <= 16
  • words[i] consists of lowercase English letters.
  • Not stated in the source; reasonable bounds.
